screen: The pipeline, with the wait on every card

markers.title: The wait is on the card, not in a report
markers.finding: The wait for a first human touch ran from days to weeks, and no one in the business could see it while it was happening. It surfaced only in exit data, long after the person had gone.
markers.decision: Every card carries how long that person has been waiting. It is the one number that appears on every card in the product.
markers.rejected: A time-to-hire figure on a monthly dashboard, which is the same number arriving too late to act on.

markers.title: The card names the owner and the start, not just the delay
markers.finding: Managers could not distinguish a candidate they had not looked at from one who was stuck behind a check somebody else owned.
markers.decision: The card says who owes the next step and since when: payroll review since Monday, one visa photo needed. The stat card underneath says the same, so the manager knows it is not theirs to chase and what they can do, which is message the candidate.
markers.rejected: One amber state for everything slow, which tells a manager to chase something that is not theirs to chase.

markers.title: A person is in one column
markers.finding: Two earlier concept screens carried the same record in two states at once, and it was spotted by eye before any check did.
markers.decision: One card per person, with the trail underneath. Tia's speed from Monday to Friday is shown as history on her card rather than as four copies of her across the board.
markers.rejected: Drawing the candidate at every stage they have passed, which looks busier and is wrong.

markers.title: An empty column says so
markers.finding: Sparse boards get padded with placeholder records, and a manager then cannot tell real volume from decoration.
markers.decision: Three columns are empty, and they say nobody is here. Two candidates is what a single restaurant's week looks like.
markers.rejected: Filling the board out, which would have meant inventing people and lying about volume to make a screenshot look impressive.
